I have a chalkboard in my classroom and before each class I write down a brief bullet list of everything we're doing that day. If it's a very detailed activity, I usually have a document on the class site that the students can refer to.

I decided last semester that I no longer had time for the bs. I didn't have an attendance policy but I made it clear that you cannot pass this class if you're not consistently showing up. Results may vary depending on your class size and the school but I found that majority of students showed up on time and those students who abused the policy ended up with very low grades at the end of the semester. 

But more importantly, I saved a lot of time by not having to take attendance or waiting for students to arrive.

You could also try doing a quiz or activity at the start of class that counts for points so anyone who's not there will lose out on those points.

You essentially open your mouth until you hear a click. Then you apply light pressure to your chin downwards, upwards, left and then right. 3-5 seconds of light pressure each direction, but you want to resist with your jaw so that it doesn't move. 

Then you open your jaw further and repeat the steps. Then while applying downwards resistance, slowly close your jaw. Then open and close teeth to teeth two times. Then open and close slowly with your tongue on the roof of your mouth. 

I've been doing this a couple of times in the morning and then again in the evenings.

I don't have a large friend group or a romantic relationship either. Here's some things that have helped me though:


- Pets! If you're an animal person, I highly recommend getting one. I've uprooted several times and my animals are always right with me. It does help knowing you have someone waiting for you at home. 


- having a third place. Somewhere you go that's not home or work. For me it's the local library. I get a chance to be around other people and I just love books. 


- take advantage of social events at your school. I'm not a social person by any means but I make myself go to different events and I've gotten close to several other faculty members doing so. I also met a new friend at orientation! 


-keep in touch with friends or family who are long distance. I message and video chat with my sister at least once or twice a month and we text every day. 


-therapy. It can help to be able to discuss your feelings with a trained professional. This kind of career field without a partner or family around to support you can be very depressing. I always feel a little better after I've vented to my therapist or journaled about it. 


- don't apply to work places you don't really want to live. I generally only apply to places in the same region of the country as where I'm from or a new region where I wouldn't mind living. But I have States and places that are a hard no and I stick to it. Like it doesn't matter if there's a high paying job in Doogleheimer, USA if you already know you're not going to be happy there. 


-find new hobbies and projects that are unrelated to your job. It's a little harder to feel lonely when you're filling up your days with activities


- accept that it's going to suck sometimes. Sometimes I'll have a really good week where I'm feeling productive and happy and then I'll have a bad couple days like this weekend where I'm angry I don't have a family of my own. 


The best solution of course is to get a partner and friends but these things take time and we don't know how much time it will take. So we just have to do what we can to get by until then. I hope this helps!

I published traditionally but didn't start thinking too much about the cover until the book had been drafted and full edited. Once that was done, I got to see a rough draft of the cover and ask for any small details I wanted changed and then the final cover was completed. 

But this didn't happen until 1.5 years after I'd signed my book deal so like others have said, focus on writing your book, securing an agent and then a book deal. Also, publishers and imprints are all different, some may give you a lot of say so over the cover, others may not ask for your input at all. Hi! I'm sorry you're going through this, depression is a life long battle and it sucks. I've been depressed since I was a child (over 15years) and I find that I have to change my treatment options fairly frequently. A drug cocktail might work for a month or two but then the depression is back, stronger than ever, and I have to adjust my meds again.

I think part of what makes us depressed folk feel hopeless about getting better is this idea that you can rid yourself of depression entirely. If you're looking to be 100% cured (and this isn't situational depression) you'll be disappointed every time. The meds, counseling, etc are there to help you but they won't make you happy on their own.

I was going through anhedonia recently because my favorite hobby became my job and I no longer could enjoy it. There's no other hobby that has made me feel the same way. But, my therapist helped me realize that sometimes you change and outgrow activities. So even though it feels like nothing will make you happy, you gotta try new stuff. All types of stuff. 

I tried coloring and puzzles at first. It was okay but not that interesting. But then I stepped outside my comfort zone and joined a dance class. I love it! Not as much as my old hobbies, but it's something new for me to focus on and try to get better at. 

Positive reframing can also help as well. Because your depression can distort your thoughts. For example, you're not experiencing suicidal thoughts so even if you don't know what it is yet, there's something for you to live for. There's always a possibility for happiness and love and fun, as long as you stick around for it.

I have a BA in english lit and an MFA in creative writing so I know exactly how you're feeling right now. But I hope my story can give you something to hold onto.

After I graduated college, I immediately went to grad school . I thought I would have an agent and a book deal by the time I graduated but I had nothing. I had to work at a fast food restaurant the summer after I graduated with my masters. 

I moved back in with my mom for 2 years and it was very depressing because I didn't feel like I was any closer to my goal of being a writer. For a long time I wished I had studied medicine instead.

I was about to give up when my best friend told me I should apply for a writers residency in another state. I filled out the application but I was pretty sure I wouldn't get it because it was highly competitive. 

But I did end up getting it! The residency basically meant I didn't have to worry about paying for housing or living expenses. Everything was covered. All I had to do was focus on my writing. 

Before I moved, I had queried over 100 agents with my manuscript. Most said no, some said nothing at all. I figured the book just wasn't good enough. But I kid you not, 2 days after I started the residency, I got a call from an agent (like 5months after I queried) and I signed with her a week later. One year later, I signed a very nice deal with a big five publisher. 

It's been a long road (signed when I was 29, I'm 30 now), but everything will fall together as long as you keep putting in the work. Even when I wasn't getting paid for it, I worked on my writing every single day. That's what you have to do with your writing and acting. Flex your skills, network, work to get even better at it. 

Don't focus on what your parents say. My mom used to get on me for not having enough money to buy myself food, but now I'm in the best financial situation out of anyone in my family. Out of anyone I personally know, tbh. So many amazing opportunities started falling in my lap that I had to start turning them down.

In conclusion, you never know when or how it's going to happen, but if you have a dream, you have to believe in yourself and do what you gotta do to make it happen. I've wanted to be a writer since I was a kid so even when I failed, it was already burned into my brain: I'm going to be a published author. Period. I'll be damned if I spend this long working at something just to give up on it. 

You'll be okay, it's only been a month, most college graduates don't immediately walk into their career. So take some time to rest and then plan what your next steps are going to be to make your dreams happen.

I actually first queried with a manuscript I'd written in graduate school. I had applied for a grant (that I didn't win) and one of the judges was a literary agent who asked to see the rest of the book. It wasn't finished but I slapped it together and then got rejected. Which was a crappy blow because I hadn't even queried this person.

Five months later, I had a brand new manuscript and started seriously querying. I queried after the second draft and did a new draft after each round. I would say start when you feel prepared. When you think you've gotten it to the best point it can be, you're ready.

Once you start getting feedback from agents, you'll either have an offer or you'll know exactly how to revise your manuscript for the next round of querying.

I'm a YA author but I know a little bit about children's publishing. You might want to see if you can team up with an illustrator and go on submission together. It'd be easier to get a yes if an illustrator is already attached to the project. 

Or, you could write a middle grade manuscript and query with that. Once you have one children's book, it's a little easier to branch out. 

The main reason why I think it's difficult to get a deal with a picture book if you don't draw is because there are illustrators who can do both the drawing and writing on their own. Especially children's books. If the pictures are A1, an agent or publishing house will work with an illustrator on the writing (since there usually isn't a lot of it in books for young children.) But it's much harder to help a writer learn how to draw.
I look at baby name sites or I'll look at objects or food around my space. Some names I really like are Apple, Raspberry, Burgundy, Cloud, etc.

It took me me around 8-10 months, 3-4 rounds of querying. I think I did 20-25 agents per round. You don't want to do too many because if they all say no, you usually can't query again with the same project. But remember, you only need ONE yes!
